scenes.heading: Two ways to bond
scenes.narration: Chemical bonds come in two main flavours. Ionic bonding and covalent bonding both join atoms together, but they do it by completely different mechanisms, and the results differ sharply.

scenes.heading: Transfer versus sharing
scenes.narration: The core difference is mechanism. Ionic bonding transfers electrons outright from one atom to another, creating charged ions, while covalent bonding shares an electron pair between both partners equally.

scenes.heading: Who bonds with whom
scenes.narration: Ionic bonding pairs a metal with a nonmetal across a large electronegativity gap, giving a rigid lattice of ions. Covalent bonding joins two nonmetals together into discrete separate molecules.

scenes.heading: Melting points and conduction
scenes.narration: Properties follow directly. Ionic solids need very high melting points and conduct electricity once molten or dissolved, while covalent molecules melt at low temperatures and usually do not conduct.

scenes.heading: One axis two answers
scenes.narration: Remember the pairing. Sodium chloride transfers electrons and forms an ionic lattice, while water shares electrons and forms covalent molecules, which is why their melting points differ so much.
